glossario.simples: The time an elected person stays in office. In Portuguese: {{mandato}}.
Being elected again to the same office, right after the first term.
The votes given to candidates or parties. Blank and null votes do not count.
A new vote between only the two candidates with the most votes, when no one got enough votes in the first round. In Portuguese: {{2º turno}}.
The person elected together with the president, the governor or the mayor to take their place when needed.
The person in reserve who takes the seat when a senator, a deputy or a city councilor leaves. In Portuguese: {{suplente}}.
The group that runs together in an election, like the candidate for mayor and their vice. In Portuguese: {{chapa}}.
A way of electing in which the seats are divided among the parties according to the votes of each one.
The branch that governs: it puts the laws into practice and takes care of public services.
The name of the monthly salary of elected officials, ministers and judges. In Portuguese: {{subsídio}}.
The highest salary anyone can receive in public service. In Portuguese: {{teto}} (“ceiling”).
A decision of Congress on matters that only Congress decides, without going to the president.
The branch that makes the laws and oversees the people who govern.
A person chosen by the president to take care of an area of the government, like health or education.
People chosen by the governor or the mayor to take care of an area, like health in the state or in the city.
{{Supremo Tribunal Federal}} (Supreme Federal Court): the highest court in the country, which takes care of the Constitution.
The House where the state deputies make the state's laws. In Portuguese: {{Assembleia Legislativa}}.
The lawmaking House of the Federal District, where the district deputies work. In Portuguese: {{Câmara Legislativa}}.
The House where the city councilors make the city's laws. In Portuguese: {{Câmara Municipal}}.
An organized group of people with similar ideas that runs in elections.
Being registered as a member of a political party.
A union of two or more parties that, for at least 4 years, act as if they were just one.
{{Tribunal Superior Eleitoral}} (Superior Electoral Court): the court that organizes and takes care of elections.
To follow and check whether someone is doing the job right and following the rules.
The people who can vote.

slides.texto: Some govern, others make laws. Let's get to know each office, one by one!
They head the **Executive** branch: they put the laws into practice and take care of public services.

cards.txt: Heads the country's government and commands the Army, the Navy and the Air Force.

dados.val: More than half of the valid votes. If no one gets there, there is a runoff (second round).

cards.mais: The president is elected together with the vice president, on the same ticket. Valid votes are the ones given to candidates: blank and null votes do not count. Whoever wins the 2026 election takes office on January 5, 2027.

cards.txt: Heads the state government. The state's police forces are under the governor's command.

dados.val: Same rule as for president: there may be a runoff.

cards.mais: The governor is elected together with the vice governor. The Federal District also has a governor. Whoever wins the 2026 election takes office on January 6, 2027.

cards.txt: Heads the city government, which takes care of streets, lighting and health clinics.

dados.val: Whoever gets the most votes. There is a runoff only where there are more than 200,000 voters.

cards.mais: The mayor is elected together with the vice mayor. Today's mayors were elected in 2024 and stay until the end of 2028. The Federal District does not have a mayor.

slides.texto: They form the **Legislative** branch: they make laws and help oversee the people who govern. They can be re-elected with no limit.

cards.txt: Makes laws for the country and represents their state in the Federal Senate ({{Senado Federal}}).

dados.val: 3 per state and 3 for the DF: 81

cards.mais: Each senator is elected with 2 alternates ({{suplentes}}). Every 4 years, the Senate renews 1/3 or 2/3 of its seats. In 2026, each state chose 2 senators.

cards.txt: Makes laws for the country and represents the people in the Chamber of Deputies ({{Câmara dos Deputados}}).
cards.mais: Each state has from 8 to 70 federal deputies, depending on its population. In the proportional vote, the seats are divided among the parties according to the votes each party gets.

cards.txt: Makes the state's laws in the Legislative Assembly.
cards.mais: In the Federal District, the name is district deputy. They work in the Legislative Chamber, which has 24 deputies.

cards.txt: Makes the city's laws in the City Council ({{Câmara Municipal}}) and oversees the mayor.
cards.mais: The number of city councilors ({{vereadores}}) in each city depends on its population. The largest City Council, in São Paulo, has 55.

slides.titulo: Who takes the place of someone who leaves?
slides.texto: Every elected office has someone in reserve. The name changes depending on the office.

itens: The president, governors and mayors each have a **vice**.
The vice is elected together with them, on the same ticket.
The vice stands in for the officeholder when they cannot work.
If the office becomes vacant for good, the vice takes over until the end of the term of office.
colunas.exemplo: If the mayor leaves office, the vice mayor takes over: she becomes the mayor.

itens: Each senator is elected with 2 **alternates**, on the same ticket.
Deputies and city councilors: the alternate is the next most-voted candidate from the same party or federation.
The alternate takes over when the seat becomes free or when the officeholder is away for a long time.
colunas.exemplo: If deputy Ana becomes a minister, the alternate from her party takes her seat.

slides.texto: The president, governors and mayors put together a team. These people are **not elected**: they are chosen.

itens.txt: The president chooses the **ministers**. Each one takes care of an area, like health or education.
The governor chooses the state secretaries.
The mayor chooses the city secretaries.
Whoever chooses them can also replace them at any time.
To be a minister, you must be Brazilian and over 21.

slides.coruja: A government minister is different from an STF minister. The STF one is a judge!

slides.titulo: How many elected officials does Brazil have?
slides.texto: Adding up all the offices and the vices, there are more than **71,000** seats. Most of them are for city councilors.
slides.nota: In government: 1 president, 27 governors and 5,569 mayors, each with a vice. Seats counted in the data of the TSE (Superior Electoral Court) for the 2024 and 2026 elections, checked on October 15, 2026.

slides.titulo: How much do elected officials earn?
slides.texto: The salary of the office is called the **official salary** ({{subsídio}}). The amounts are for 2026, before deductions, in reais (R$), Brazil's currency.

itens.txt: President, vice president, ministers, federal deputies and senators: R$ 46,366.19 a month.
This amount is set by Congress itself, through a legislative decree.
State deputy: at most 75% of the federal deputy's official salary.
City councilor: at most 20% to 75% of the state deputy's official salary, depending on the size of the city.
**Salary cap**: by the rules, no public salary can be higher than that of an STF minister (also R$ 46,366.19).

slides.coruja: The salaries of the governor and of the mayor are set by state and city laws.

slides.titulo: Why does every candidate have a party?
slides.texto: A **party** is an organized group of people with similar ideas about how to take care of the country.

itens.txt: In Brazil, only people with **party membership**, that is, who are registered in a party, can be candidates.
That is why there are no candidates without a party.
Anyone can create a party, as long as they follow the rules. The country has many parties, with different ideas.
Every party must be national and register its rules with the TSE, the elections court.
Two or more parties can form a party federation and act as if they were just one.

slides.coruja: Made-up example: the Circle Party wants more playgrounds; the Square Party wants more buses. Each voter chooses who they agree with.

slides.pergunta: How many years does a senator's term of office last?
slides.explica: A senator stays in office for 8 years. The other elected offices last 4 years.
Ministers are not elected. The president chooses them and can replace them at any time.
